title: How Drones and Information Warfare Are Reshaping India-Pakistan Crises
author: Saima Afzal
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/ian-usher-
JPAfSd_acI8-unsplash-680x383.jpg)

Image by Ian Usher.

Just weeks after South Asia stepped back from one of its most serious military
crises in recent years, fresh tensions in the [Poonch
sector](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O4fhO8LMQvw) highlighted how rapidly
the region's security environment is changing. The military [confrontation of
May 2025](https://www.stimson.org/2025/four-days-in-may-the-india-pakistan-
crisis-of-2025/) demonstrated how quickly local incidents can escalate into
broader strategic crises between India and Pakistan. While the subsequent
ceasefire reduced immediate tensions, it did little to address the mistrust
that continues to define relations between the two nuclear-armed neighbors.

Since partition in 1947, Kashmir has remained the principal flashpoint between
India and Pakistan, generating wars, military standoffs and periodic
escalations that continue to shape South Asia's security environment. The
events of [June 9 in the Poonch
sector](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/6/9/deadly-protests-in-pakistan-
administered-kashmir-whats-going-on) provide a revealing case study of how
these crises are evolving.

According to Pakistan, Indian forces engaged in aggressive military posturing
despite repeated calls for restraint, while Indian officials alleged a
Pakistani [drone incursion](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DZXi6SESIEi/).
Islamabad rejected the accusation, arguing that such claims reflected a
familiar pattern of narrative construction designed to justify military
pressure and shape international perceptions.

Whether one accepts Pakistan's interpretation or India's, the significance of
the incident lies elsewhere. The Poonch episode demonstrates how modern crises
are increasingly shaped by drones, information competition and compressed
decision-making timelines. Within hours of the incident, competing narratives
were circulating across official channels, television networks and social
media platforms, long before independent verification was possible.

The speed with which competing narratives emerged after the [June 9
incident](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/6/9/deadly-protests-in-pakistan-
administered-kashmir-whats-going-on) reflected a pattern already visible
during the May 2025 crisis. Within hours of military exchanges and official
statements, television networks, government spokespersons and social media
accounts on both sides were presenting sharply different interpretations of
events. Long before independent verification became possible, public opinion
had already begun to harden around competing narratives.

This acceleration of the information cycle is becoming a defining feature of
contemporary security crises. In previous decades, governments often had days
to assess developments before public pressure demanded a response. Today,
leaders may face expectations to react within hours, creating a widening gap
between the speed of information and the speed of verification.

**The Rise of Instant Narrative Warfare**

The June 9 incident followed a pattern already visible during the May 2025
crisis. Competing official narratives emerged almost immediately as
governments sought to shape international opinion, reassure domestic audiences
and establish political legitimacy. Social media accelerated this process,
allowing claims and counterclaims to spread faster than traditional
verification mechanisms could respond.

The result is a security environment in which perception often develops faster
than evidence. Information has become an [operational
domain](https://cenjows.in/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/GL_Report_18_Sep_25.pdf)
alongside land, air, sea, space and cyberspace. Managing a crisis now requires
governments to compete simultaneously on military, diplomatic and
informational fronts.

This process carries risks. Once leaders publicly commit to a particular
narrative, the space for compromise narrows. As a result, incidents that might
once have remained localized can quickly acquire broader strategic
significance.

**Drones Are Changing the Escalation Equation**

The June 9 allegations also illustrate why drones are becoming increasingly
important in crisis dynamics between India and Pakistan.

Unlike traditional ceasefire violations, drone-related incidents often involve
uncertainty regarding attribution and intent. In the Poonch case, competing
claims emerged almost immediately, while definitive verification remained
elusive. This gap between accusation and verification is becoming one of the
defining characteristics of modern security crises.

The strategic implications are significant. The shorter the interval between
allegation and response, the greater the risk that political and military
decisions will be made before facts are fully established. In highly charged
security environments, leaders often face pressure to demonstrate resolve
before investigations are complete. Under such conditions, misperception can
become a driver of escalation in its own right.

The June 9 episode demonstrates how [emerging
technologies](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6308358) can
compress crisis timelines and increase the possibility that uncertainty,
rather than intent, shapes decision-making. For military planners, drones
provide surveillance and reconnaissance advantages. For policymakers, however,
they introduce a different challenge: ambiguity. In a region marked by
longstanding mistrust, ambiguity can itself become a source of instability.

**Why Deterrence Alone Is No Longer Enough**

The recurring tensions along the [Line of
Control](https://www.stimson.org/2014/deterrence-stability-and-reducing-
nuclear-dangers-south-asia/) expose the limitations of deterrence as a
foundation for lasting stability.

Deterrence has helped prevent large-scale war between India and Pakistan, but
it has not eliminated recurring confrontations. The [2021
ceasefire](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13533312.2021.1894934)
understanding demonstrated that reductions in violence are possible when
stability serves the interests of both governments. Yet maintaining such
stability requires more than military restraint. It requires communication
channels, crisis-management mechanisms and procedures capable of preventing
misunderstandings from escalating into larger confrontations.

That task is becoming more difficult. Emerging technologies, rapid information
dissemination and growing public scrutiny are compressing the time available
for decision-makers to assess events and formulate responses.

**A Challenge Extending Beyond South Asia**

The security dilemmas highlighted by the June 9 incident are not unique to
India and Pakistan. Along the India-China frontier and in the South China Sea,
governments are increasingly relying on drones and information operations
while confronting similar problems of ambiguity, attribution and rapid
escalation.

Although the geopolitical contexts differ, a common challenge is emerging.
Technology is accelerating the pace of crises while reducing the time
available for verification and diplomacy. Whether the setting is the Line of
Control, the Himalayan frontier or contested waters in the South China Sea,
governments are increasingly confronting the same question: how to prevent
ambiguity and misperception from escalating into confrontation.

The June 9 incident should therefore be viewed not merely as another episode
in the India-Pakistan rivalry, but as part of a broader transformation in how
security crises unfold across Asia.

Pakistan maintains that while it seeks peace and regional stability, it will
continue to defend its sovereignty and security interests against any
perceived threat. Yet the larger lesson extends beyond the immediate dispute.
Future India-Pakistan crises are likely to be shaped as much by information
competition and technological ambiguity as by conventional military activity.

The challenge facing policymakers is changing. Preventing conflict remains
essential, but preventing miscalculation may prove equally important. In the
past, escalation along the Line of Control was measured primarily through
troop deployments and artillery exchanges. Increasingly, it is being measured
by the speed of a drone, the reach of a social media narrative and the
shrinking amount of time leaders have to distinguish fact from perception.

In future crises, the greatest danger may not be what governments know. It may
be how quickly they feel compelled to act before they know enough.
